profile.name: Tobas
profile.tagline: A high-energy Bolivian folk dance of warrior jumps and vibrant feathered costumes.
profile.insight: Created in 1905 Oruro by miners inspired by Tarija pilgrims, the Tobas dance transformed a pejorative label into a national symbol of indigenous warrior strength and agility.
profile.profile: Tobas is a vibrant Bolivian folk dance originating in the mining centers of Oruro in the early 20th century. It is characterized by high-energy, acrobatic jumps and movements that emulate the hunting and warrior traditions of the Toba people of the Chaco. Recognized as national heritage, the dance is performed at major events like the Carnaval de Oruro, featuring elaborate feathered costumes and rhythmic brass music.
profile.profile_long:
The Tobas dance emerged in the early 20th century within the mining centers of Oruro, Bolivia. Its origins are traced to 1905, when Tomás Cáceres Nava and his son, Donato Cáceres Véliz, returned to Oruro after witnessing the 'Chunchos' dance at the religious festival of San Roque in Tarija. Inspired by the performance, they formed a 'comparsa' (dance group) that would evolve into the Tobas. The name itself was not chosen by the creators but was adopted from the public, who used it to refer to the group after the 1882 death of French explorer Jules Crevaux, allegedly killed by the Toba people of the Chaco region. Despite the name, the dance holds little direct relation to the Toba people themselves, serving instead as an urban reinterpretation of indigenous warrior aesthetics.

Throughout the 20th century, the dance underwent significant development. In 1917, the 'Comparsa de Tobas de Oruro' was officially organized with the support of local miners. Later, in 1945, artist Cristóbal Franco founded the 'Comparsa Tobas Zona Central,' and in 1984, groups like the 'Comparsa de Tobas San José' were reorganized to preserve the tradition. The music accompanying the dance has shifted over time; while it originally relied on traditional Andean instruments like pinquillos and quenas, it transitioned to brass instrumentation around 1960, providing a more agile and energetic soundscape.

The choreography of Tobas is defined by its athleticism. Dancers perform a series of acrobatic jumps and movements that simulate hunting, stalking, and combat. Each step is named and carries specific meaning: the 'Bolivar' involves fast, regular jumps; the 'Cambá' features high jumps reaching up to one meter; the 'Chucu-chucu' uses a rapid rhythm performed on the tiptoes; and the 'Paso de la flecha' represents the courage and strength of ethnic groups seeking freedom. Other steps, such as the 'Combate de tribus,' depict the confrontation between tribes to maintain cultural independence.

The visual identity of the dance is equally striking. Performers wear elaborate costumes that include headwear made entirely of feathers, decorated with jewels. Their attire consists of skirts and tops adorned with colorful fabrics, beads, and fringes. A signature element is the use of cow or lamb hooves sewn onto fabric bands tied around the ankles, which create a rhythmic sound as the dancers move. Dancers often carry spears, hatchets, or other symbolic weapons. The presence of 'hechiceros' (shamans or sorcerers) in masks and carrying staves adds a layer of spiritual representation, connecting the dancers to the 'spirit of the world.'

Today, Tobas is a prominent feature of the Bolivian cultural landscape, performed at major events such as the Carnaval de Oruro and the Fiesta del Gran Poder. On March 24, 2014, the Bolivian government officially declared the dance as tangible and intangible heritage of the nation. Every January 24th, Bolivia celebrates the national day of the Tobas dance, ensuring its continued practice and visibility in both national and international festivities, including those in Chile, Peru, and Argentina.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance was created in Oruro around 1905 by Tomás and Donato Cáceres Nava, inspired by the Chunchos of Tarija. It was officially organized in 1917 and gained national heritage status in 2014.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is highly acrobatic, featuring jumps and hunting-themed gestures. Specific steps include the Bolivar (fast jumps), Cambá (high jumps), Chucu-chucu (tiptoe rhythm), and the Paso de la flecha.
sections.music_and_instruments: Originally performed with pinquillos and quenas, the music transitioned to brass instruments in 1960 to achieve greater agility and energy.
sections.costume_and_setting: Costumes feature feathered headwear, beaded skirts and tops, and ankle bands made with cow or lamb hooves. Dancers carry spears or hatchets.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance represents warrior energy, hunting, and the preservation of indigenous identity. It is performed at the Carnaval de Oruro and other religious festivals.
sections.notable_figures: Tomás Cáceres Nava, Donato Cáceres Véliz, Juan Manuel Cuellar Carpio, Cristóbal Franco, Mateo Escalera Bravo, Carlos Feliciano Lenis.
sections.lineage: Derived from the Chunchos dance of Tarija.

profile.sacred_note: Not described in sources as a sacred dance, though it involves shamanic characters and is performed at religious festivals.

basic_steps: Camba: High jumps reaching up to one meter.
Chucu-chucu: Rapid rhythm performed on tiptoes.
Paso de la flecha: War-themed step representing courage.
teaching.level_notes: Requires high physical strength, stamina, and coordination.

music_profile.sound_description: Originally flute-based (pinquillos and quenas), the modern sound is defined by agile brass instrumentation.

movement_profile.footwork: Includes jumps and tiptoe movements; ankle hooves provide percussive sound.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Gestures emulate throwing spears or hunting.

signature_moves.name: Cambá
signature_moves.description: High jumps reaching up to one meter.
